title: Colour each mark for its meaning
statement: Choose a mark's colour for what the mark means, never by its order in a list.
detail: The style notes for the unit videos say to use red and green to mark the meaning of a word or claim (`g9/tools/unit-video-essay/INTEGRATION.md`, line 21), and the quotation card's notes ask that each mark's `meaning` say why a span is marked, not just its colour (`g9-unit-video-packages/quote-card/README.md`, line 31). The lesson engine instead gives a quotation's marked words red, ochre and green by their order (`g9/transformer/src/video/beats.js`, line 16), so in its film on a speech the word for what was said came out red and the word for what was done ochre, whatever each word does (`g9-transformer-runs/blocks/34c293906aa945a2.json`, lines 17-22). No lesson has been reviewed by a person or used by a student, so what viewers read into the colours has not been measured (`g9/transformer/README.md`, line 120).
against: Colouring by column is the reference's design and the module's: "A two-column red/green argument map." (`g9/tools/unit-video-essay/INTEGRATION.md`, line 12), "The left and right columns have stable semantic colors" (`g9-unit-video-packages/argument-map/README.md`, line 3), and in the engine's two-readings frame the first reading always gets the red edge, "const accent = left ? '#db796f' : '#8bbf9a';" (`g9-unit-video-packages/argument-map/src/index.js`, line 68), though both readings are meant to be defensible; whether that reads as a verdict on one of them is not measured.

evidence.quote: Use red and green to mark the *meaning* of a word or claim, and keep marks and arrows quiet enough that the source remains legible.
Use `meaning` to describe why a span is marked, not just its color.
